relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: At death's edge, David transfers not only a throne but unfinished loyalties and vendettas.
Mortality is universal, yet David frames strength through a command to perform manhood.
Solomon is called to Torah-shaped leadership rather than personal appetite.
The dynasty is made conditional upon truthful, whole-hearted conduct.
David names Joab's murders in peacetime, blood that royal convenience never fully addressed.
He delegates lethal revenge to Solomon under the name of wisdom.
Debt of care toward Barzillai's children is carried into the new reign.
David remembers Shimei's protest and the oath by which he promised not to kill him.
The dying king preserves the words of his oath while transferring its bloodshed to his heir.
David dies and is buried inside the city bearing his name.
Forty years of reign are condensed into a number, leaving the harmed and helped to carry the detail.
Solomon inherits a throne already surrounded by instructions for removal.
Bathsheba receives Adonijah cautiously because royal family conversation can become lethal.
He asks permission to place a request before her.
Adonijah narrates his lost claim as both popular expectation and Divine reversal.
He seeks access to Solomon through the king's mother.
Abishag's body becomes the language through which a former claimant reaches again toward kingship.
Bathsheba agrees to carry the request, though her reasons remain unstated.
Solomon honors his mother publicly with a seat beside the throne.
He promises not to refuse before hearing what she asks.
Bathsheba repeats the marriage request while Abishag remains voiceless.
Solomon reads the request as a dynastic maneuver rather than a woman's marriage.
A royal oath turns interpretation into a death sentence.
Solomon invokes Divine establishment to authorize immediate execution.
Benaiah kills Adonijah, converting succession anxiety into irreversible state violence.
Abiathar is threatened with death but exiled to his land because of prior sacred and political service.
Priestly removal is narrated as prophetic fulfillment, yet it also clears a rival institution from Solomon's court.
Joab seeks sanctuary at the altar after hearing the purge has reached his coalition.
Solomon orders killing inside sacred space.
Joab refuses to leave, forcing the regime to decide whether sanctuary restrains royal vengeance.
Solomon chooses execution and burial, claiming the act will cleanse his house of Joab's blood.
The murdered commanders are named as more righteous than their killer.
Bloodguilt is pushed onto Joab's descendants while perpetual peace is claimed for David's line.
Benaiah kills Joab at the altar and the body is carried to burial.
The executor receives the army, and the surviving priest receives the high office.
Shimei is confined to Jerusalem under a lethal boundary.
Movement across one stream is made punishable by death.
Under royal threat, Shimei accepts the condition.
Two servants escape, creating a conflict between their freedom and Shimei's confinement.
Shimei crosses the boundary to reclaim them.
The surveillance system reports his journey to Solomon.
The king recites the oath and the threatened consequence.
Religious oath language is used to frame violation of royal confinement.
Solomon joins the boundary breach to Shimei's former protest against David.
Dynastic blessing is set opposite the condemned man's death.
Benaiah executes Shimei, and the narrator calls the blood-secured throne established.

contemplative_note: The chapter exposes how a kingdom may call itself established when rivals are dead, priests displaced, critics confined, women assigned, and executioners promoted. Wisdom must be measured by more than successful consolidation.
